https://www.myjoyonline.com/vision-fc-en.body: Vision FC ended a six-game winless run in the Ghana Premier League with a convincing 3-1 victory over Dreams FC at the Tuba AstroTurf on Sunday. The visitors made a flying start to the match, scoring three goals in the opening 26 minutes to secure their second win of the 2026/27 campaign. Sherif Mohammed opened the scoring in the 12th minute before Setsofia Agetey doubled Vision’s advantage five minutes later. Mohammed then completed his brace in the 26th minute to give Vision a commanding 3-0 lead before the break. Dreams FC responded in the second half, pulling one back in the 58th minute through an own goal by Ibrahim Larbi. However, Vision held on to claim all three points and end their disappointing run since winning their opening league fixture. The result leaves Dreams FC rooted to the bottom of the league table with three points after eight matches, having recorded three draws and five defeats without a win this season. Vision, meanwhile, move to ninth place with nine points from eight matches. They have now recorded two wins, three draws and three defeats. The victory provides a timely boost for Vision as they seek to build momentum in the league, while Dreams FC face mounting pressure to turn their fortunes around after another disappointing outing

Unlock these with Subscription The ecologically fragile Nilgiris district in Tamil Nadu was hit by as many as 62 landslips in the 24 hours ending at 7 a.m. on Sunday (October 25, 2026), following light to moderate spell of rain across the district. According to official data from the district administration, heavy damage to infrastructure was reported, with 15 huts partly damaged, one hut fully collapsed and 16 revetments damaged across the district. The continuous spell led to the damage of two high-tension poles, nine low-tension poles and one distribution transformer. A total of 28 trees were uprooted. The district recorded a cumulative total rainfall of 453.9 mm during the 24-hour period, with an overall average rainfall of 14.64 mm. Ten out of the 31 rain gauge statins in the district received moderate rain, with the remaining locations recorded light rain in the 24 hours. Parsons Valley in Udhagamandalam taluk recorded the highest rainfall in the district at 52 mm, followed by Upper Bhavani in Kundah taluk at 38 mm and Naduvattam and Glenmorgan (also in Udhagamandalam taluk) at 37 mm each. The district had 19 landslips in the previous 24 hours ending on Saturday (October 24) morning. Traffic along Mettupalayam-Coonoor stretch remains suspended and vehicles are being allowed to and fro Nilgiris along Mettupalayam-Kotagiri Road between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m., said police sources. People who want to travel to Coonoor and Udhagamandalam (Ooty) from Mettupalayam and vice versa must use Kotagiri Road during the permitted hours. Tourism activities in the Nilgiris also remain suspended for three days from Saturday. Several parts of the Nilgiris received heavy rains from Sunday afternoon and continued through the night. As a result, new landslips were reported on the Coonoor-Mettupalayam ghat section. A man and his son suffered injuries after a tree fell onto their house at Ketti in the district. A huge tree fell onto a stationary car near Rose Garden at Udhagamandalam town, which received heavy rain in the evening. On Avalanche road, a tree fell onto a house. Trees were uprooted at several other locations. The landslip site near Burliyar on the Mettupalayam-Udhagamandalam Road, where a TNSTC bus was caught under the debris on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, resulting in the driver being killed and the conductor injured, continues to remain in a precarious condition. Authorities are concerned about large boulders that may fall from the slope in the event of an extreme or heavy rainfall. Officials from the Department of Geology and Mining visited the place on Sunday, where the debris from the road has been removed. However, work could not be continued for long due to the rain. “It is a very tricky terrain. The boulders remaining on the slope have to be dealt with very carefully. Experts are evaluating how to remove them safely without causing more damage to the road,” Coimbatore Collector Pavankumar G. Giriyappanavar told The Hindu . He said embankments of the ghat section were found damaged at four places between Mettupalayam and Burliyar during an assessment carried out on Sunday. Crash barriers and the road surface were also found damaged in some places. “Temporary restoration works have been completed at places where embankments were damaged. Considering heavy vehicle movement on the road, which connects to Udhagamandalam, a team of experts from the office of the Commissioner of Revenue Administration, Chennai, inspected the stretch between Mettupalayam and Burliyar on Sunday. The experts will give us a comprehensive idea of the places where works, including restorations, have to be carried out,” he said. The team also identified a few places that were prone to landslip and falling trees. Mr. Giriyappanavar said the team would evaluate the entire stretch between Mettupalayam and Udhagamandalam. “They will assess and tell us what all the temporary works needed to be carried out to restore the traffic,” he said. According to him, since the road was under the control of the National Highways, a team from the National Highways Regional Office in Chennai would visit the entire stretch on Monday (October 26, 2026). “Since there is an orange alert, and the rainfall is also heavy for the next couple of days, we want to leave no stone unturned. We will be able to allow the traffic until the assessment is completed and we get a clearance from the National Highways,” Mr. Giriyappanavar added. Owing to the rain and obstructions caused by landslips, Southern Railway has suspended Nilgiri Mountain Railway (NMR) services between Mettupalayam and Coonoor from Saturday. Services between the two stations were suspended from Saturday, following a spell of heavy overnight rain, triggering fall of trees and debris onto the track. Sources with the Salem Division said that obstructions caused by landslips and fall of boulders and trees across the track have been reported at over 25 places. Though works were underway to remove the obstructions, incessant rain was resulting in fresh obstructions. However, train services between Coonoor and Udhagamandalam were not affected, said the sources. https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/s.summary: Unlock these with Subscription The Supreme Court recently held in The State of Andhra Pradesh vs Suda Suresh Veera Venkata Naga Raju that Section 187(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), enlarges the window during which police custody may be sought by the investigating agency. https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/s.body: Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription The Supreme Court recently held in The State of Andhra Pradesh vs Suda Suresh Veera Venkata Naga Raju that Section 187(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), enlarges the window during which police custody may be sought by the investigating agency. Such custody, under the BNSS is now available in parts, though in aggregate not exceeding 15 days during the first 40 or 60 days of the total permissible period of detention, rather than being confined to the first 15 days of remand alone. The Court also held that though the right to meet an advocate of choice is guaranteed under Section 38 of the BNSS, it does not, by any means contemplate the continuous ongoing physical presence of an advocate for the entirety of each interrogation session. In a case of custodial death in which the dead body of the deceased-victim remained untraced, the original hard disks of the CCTV system were yet to be discovered, and discoveries under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) were imminent, the judicial magistrate granted eight days of police custody (against the requested 12 days), and allowed the accused to nominate two advocates of his choice to be present during police custody. Out of the two advocates, one was allowed to be present at any given point of time during investigation. The order clearly stated that ‘under no circumstances shall the period of police custody granted under this order be extended’. While on appeal, the Andhra Pradesh High Court modified some conditions pertaining to the period of police custody and presence of an advocate throughout the probe. The State therefore challenged the above conditions in the Supreme Court on the premise that these directly impinged upon the rights of the investigating officer to conduct unhindered investigation. The Supreme Court held that the apprehensions expressed by the investigating agency were realistic and justified and the statutory scheme under the BNSS which enlarges the window of police custody, must also be borne in mind. A magistrate or a court while exercising its supervisory jurisdiction, cannot place an absolute and non-extendable outer limit on custody, since such a limit forecloses recourse to Section 187(2) of the BNSS, regardless of what the investigation may yet reveal. The Court therefore permitted 7 days of (additional) police custody so that the total period of police remand, including that granted by the lower courts would not exceed 15 days. Section 58 of the BNSS provides that any person arrested by the police without warrant cannot be detained for more than 24 hours, unless authorised by a magistrate under Section 187. Section 187(3) provides that the magistrate may authorise the (judicial) detention of an accused person beyond the period of 15 days, if he is satisfied that adequate grounds exist for doing so, for a period exceeding – (i) 90 days, where the investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of 10 years or more; (ii) 60 days, where the investigation relates to any other offence. Thus, in case the probe is not completed within the above stipulated time period, the accused person may be released, which is widely known as default bail. The Supreme Court in the Suda Suresh case held that this legislative change was intended to meet situations where fresh facts, discoveries or leads may emerge during the course of investigation. Therefore, the window of police remand was enlarged beyond the initial 15 days, up to 40 days or 60 days of investigation. Previously, Section 167 of the CrPC provided that the detention of an accused in police custody could not be granted beyond the initial 15 days in the whole. However, during this first period of 15 days the magistrate could alter the nature of the custody from judicial custody to police custody and vice versa. Section 38 of the BNSS provides that ‘when any person is arrested and interrogated by the police, he shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation’. This provision is pari materia to Section 41-D of the CrPC. The top court held that a plain reading of the provision makes it clear that it does not contemplate the continuous, ongoing physical presence of an advocate for the entirety of each interrogation session, whatever be the visual or audible distance maintained. The Court held that an unqualified entitlement to continuous presence, would travel beyond what Section 38 BNSS itself contemplates. The Court therefore modified the condition imposed by the High Court, and held that such a lawyer shall only be allowed to remain present within the site of interrogation where he can see the respondent-accused. Further, the lawyer shall not be permitted to intervene in the process of investigation at any cost. On the question of videography and CCTV documentation, the Court also held that instead of uninterrupted videography of the transit of the accused between locations, the audio-visual recording of the actual session of interrogation, and of any proceedings of discovery or recovery undertaken with the accused, will satisfy the requirement. https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/s.title_zh: 最高法院澄清BNSS下警方羁押的适用范围
https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/s.body_zh: 订阅可享独家报道、社论、观点等更多内容。订阅即可解锁这些内容。最高法院近期在《安得拉邦邦长诉苏达·苏雷什·维拉·文卡塔·纳加·拉朱》案中裁定，《 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 》（BNSS）第187(2)条扩大了侦查机关可以申请警察羁押的时间窗口。根据BNSS，这类羁押目前可分阶段适用，在总计允许的拘留期限前40天或60天内，累计不得超过15天，而非仅限于最初15天的还押期。法院还裁定，尽管BNSS第38条保障被拘留人会见其所选律师的权利，但该条并不意味着律师必须在每次讯问全程持续、亲自在场。在一起羁押死亡案中，死者的遗体尚未找到，闭路电视系统的原始硬盘也尚未被发现，而根据《 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 》（BSA）进行的搜查取证工作即将展开，司法治安法官批准了8天警察羁押（申请方要求12天），并允许被告指定两名由其选择的律师在警察羁押期间在场。这两名律师中，有一名获准在侦查期间任何特定时段在场。该命令明确规定：“在任何情况下，均不得延长根据本命令批准的警察羁押期限。”安得拉邦高等法院在上诉期间修改了有关警察羁押期限及律师在侦查全程在场等部分条件。因此，该邦以这些条件直接妨碍侦查官不受阻碍地开展侦查为由，向最高法院提出质疑。最高法院裁定，侦查机关所表达的担忧是现实且有合理依据的，同时必须考虑BNSS扩大警察羁押窗口的法定安排。治安法官或法院在行使监督管辖权时，不能对羁押设置绝对且不可延长的上限，因为无论侦查可能揭示何种情况，这一上限都会排除适用BNSS第187(2)条的可能性。因此，法院准许了7天（额外）警察羁押，使包括下级法院已批准在内的警察还押总期限不超过15天。BNSS第58条规定，任何由警方在无逮捕令情况下逮捕的人，不得被拘留超过24小时，除非根据第187条获得治安法官授权。第187(3)条规定，如治安法官确信存在充分理由，可以批准将被告的司法拘留期限延长至超过下列期限：(i) 侦查涉及可判处死刑、无期徒刑或10年及以上监禁的罪行时，为90天；(ii) 侦查涉及其他任何罪行时，为60天。因此，如侦查未能在上述规定期限内完成，被告可能被释放，这通常被称为“默认保释”。最高法院在苏达·苏雷什案中裁定，这项立法变更旨在应对侦查过程中可能出现新事实、新发现或新线索的情况。因此，警察还押窗口被扩大至最初15天以上，覆盖侦查的前40天或60天。此前，《CrPC》第167条规定，对被告的警察羁押在整个最初15天内不得获准延长。然而，在这最初的15天内，治安法官可以将羁押性质从司法羁押改为警察羁押，反之亦然。BNSS第38条规定，“任何人被警方逮捕并讯问时，均有权在讯问期间会见其所选择的律师，但并非讯问全程均可会见”。该规定与《CrPC》第41-D条内容相同。最高法院裁定，从该规定的字面解读可以看出，无论律师与讯问现场保持何种视觉或听觉距离，该条均不意味着律师必须在每次讯问全程持续、亲自在场。法院认为，不受限制地要求律师持续在场，将超出BNSS第38条本身的设想。因此，法院修改了高等法院施加的条件，裁定该律师只有在其能够看到应诉被告的情况下，才可留在讯问现场。此外，无论如何，该律师均不得介入侦查过程。关于录像及闭路电视记录问题，法院还裁定，无需对被告在不同地点之间的转移过程进行不间断录像，只需对实际讯问过程，以及在被告参与下开展的任何发现或追回程序进行视听记录，即可满足要求。评论须以英文撰写，并使用完整句子。评论不得含有辱骂性或人身攻击内容。请遵守我们的社区评论指南。我们已迁移至新的评论平台。如果你已是《The Hindu》的注册用户并已登录，可以继续参与我们的文章讨论。如尚无账户，请注册并登录后发表评论。用户登录账户后，可以查看自己在Vuukle上的历史评论

https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/t.body: Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription India’s electric mobility transition is gathering momentum. Electric vehicle adoption is rising, manufacturing investments are expanding, and policy support continues to strengthen. Meanwhile, circular economy principles are becoming increasingly embedded in India’s sustainability and industrial policy frameworks. Yet, circularity is not a single action — it is built on a hierarchy that prioritises reducing resource consumption, reusing existing assets, and recycling materials only when products have genuinely reached the end of their useful life. India’s policy framework has made important progress on the recycling dimension of this hierarchy. The Motor Vehicles (Registration and Functions of Vehicle Scrapping Facility) Rules, 2021, and the Environment Protection (End of Life Vehicles) Rules, 2025, have strengthened the framework for responsible vehicle recycling and material recovery. As of January 2026, 129 Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities were operational across 21 States and Union Territories, and 4.3 lakh vehicles had been processed through them. This represents important progress in building a formal ecosystem for vehicle recycling and resource recovery. However, circularity is not only about managing waste after it is created, but equally about preserving value before assets become waste. That’s why the principle of reuse deserves greater attention within India’s electric mobility transition. India has one of the world’s largest vehicle populations. As the country pursues transport electrification, the challenge is not only how many new electric vehicles can be sold, but also how existing vehicles can be integrated into the transition in the most resource-efficient manner. An effective scrappage policy is essential for removing vehicles that have genuinely reached the end of their useful lives. Yet, treating every ageing vehicle as a candidate for disposal risks overlooking a significant opportunity to extend asset life while simultaneously accelerating electrification. Vehicle retrofitment offers one such pathway . By replacing the internal combustion engine, fuel system, and related components of an existing vehicle with an electric powertrain, and retaining the core vehicle structure, retrofitment enables the continued use of assets that remain structurally sound. In circular economy terms, it is a practical expression of reuse. Rather than recovering value only after a vehicle becomes waste, retrofitment preserves and extends the value already embedded in the asset. The distinction is important. Recycling recovers materials. Reuse preserves functionality. A vehicle can be old yet structurally sound. It can have a polluting engine while retaining a strong chassis, intact body, and years of potential service life remaining. In such cases, retrofitting the vehicle to electric powertrain through certified technology becomes the more circular option than scrapping. This is not a competing strategy to scrappage. It is the missing middle path that policy has not focused on yet. The environmental mathematics underscore why this distinction matters. A single two-wheeler generates approximately 90 kilograms of material for recycling and 18 kilograms of landfill waste when scrapped. Scaled across India’s vehicle fleet of approximately 30 crore vehicles, a scrap-first approach would generate 2.7 crore tonnes of recyclable material alone, in addition to generating 0.54 crore tonnes of landfill waste that strains land and environmental resources. Retrofitment mitigates this burden by extending vehicle life where safety permits, thereby reducing both material demand and waste generation. This alignment with UN Sustainable Development Goal no. 12 — responsible consumption and production — is not coincidental. Retrofitment directly supports the call for sustainable consumption patterns, better resource efficiency, and reduced waste. Scrappage contributes to circularity by recovering materials from vehicles that have genuinely reached the end of their useful lives. Retrofitment contributes to circularity by preventing vehicles with structural integrity from reaching that stage prematurely. Both are necessary; the question is which pathway each vehicle follows. Policy should be designed to treat vehicles based on their condition rather than age alone. A useful starting point is a national vehicle hierarchy framework that distinguishes between three distinct pathways. The first pathway addresses vehicles that remain safe, compliant, and efficient. These should continue operating with routine maintenance. Not every older vehicle is problematic, and age alone should not trigger removal from service. The second pathway is retrofitment, which applies to vehicles with sound structural integrity but ageing, inefficient, or polluting powertrains. These vehicles can be transformed into electric vehicles through certified conversion processes, extending their useful lives while reducing emissions and fossil fuel dependence. In the third pathway, vehicles proceed to scrappage and recycling. It applies exclusively to vehicles with compromised safety, severe structural degradation, accident damage, significant corrosion, or conditions that render continued operation unsafe. Such a hierarchical framework would align India’s mobility transition with genuine circular economy principles. It would recognise that not all vehicles are alike and that policy must distinguish between assets that have exhausted their value and assets that retain substantial utility. India’s transport sector transition is not a competition between new EVs and older vehicles. Rather, it is a question about how India approaches resource efficiency during an energy transformation. The circular economy hierarchy exists for a reason. It prevents waste before it is created and recycles only after a product has genuinely reached the end of its useful life. The distinction avoids unnecessary scrappage. If India adopts an age-assessed transition pathway, it would signal that it genuinely understands this circularity principle. It would make scrappage more acceptable because citizens would perceive that older vehicles are not dismissed indiscriminately but assessed for their potential transformation. It would advance authentic circularity. India is emerging as a global leader in energy transition. It can equally lead in how transitions are managed. Not only through waste, but through wisdom. That is not simply sustainability. That is the principle that has made India’s economy resilient across centuries. https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/t.body_zh:

印度的电动交通转型正在提速。电动汽车普及率持续上升，制造投资不断扩大，政策支持也在进一步增强。与此同时，循环经济原则正日益融入印度的可持续发展和产业政策框架。然而，循环性并非单一行动，而是一套优先顺序：优先减少资源消耗、再次利用现有资产，只有当产品确实达到使用寿命终点时，才回收材料。

印度的政策框架在回收这一环节取得了重要进展。《2021年《机动车（车辆报废设施登记及职能）规则》和《2025年《环境保护（报废车辆）规则》强化了负责任车辆回收和材料回收的框架。截至2026年1月，21个邦和联邦属地共有129家注册车辆报废设施投入运营，累计处理43万辆车。这是在建设正规车辆回收和资源回收生态系统方面取得的重要进展。

然而，循环性不仅关乎废物产生后的管理，同样关乎在资产变成废物之前保存其价值。因此，在印度电动交通转型过程中，再次利用原则值得得到更多关注。

印度拥有全球规模最大的车辆保有量之一。随着该国推进交通电气化，挑战不仅在于能够销售多少辆新电动汽车，还在于如何以最具资源效率的方式将现有车辆纳入转型进程。有效的报废政策对于淘汰确实已达到使用寿命终点的车辆至关重要。然而，如果把每一辆老龄车辆都视为处置对象，就可能忽视一项重大机会，即延长资产使用寿命，同时加快电气化。

车辆改装提供了一条可行路径。通过将现有车辆的内燃机、燃料系统及相关部件替换为电动动力总成，同时保留车辆主体结构，改装可使结构仍完好的资产继续使用。用循环经济术语来说，这是对再次利用的切实体现。改装并非只在车辆成为废物后才回收其价值，而是保存并延长资产中已经蕴含的价值。这一区别十分重要：回收是回收材料，再次利用是保留功能。

一辆车即使老旧，也可能结构完好。它可能装有污染严重的发动机，但仍保有坚固的底盘、完好的车身，以及多年的潜在服役寿命。在这种情况下，通过认证技术将车辆改装为电动动力总成，就比报废更具循环性。

这并不是与报废相竞争的策略，而是政策尚未充分关注的中间路径。

环境数据凸显了这一区别的重要性。一辆两轮摩托车报废后大约会产生90千克可供回收的材料和18千克填埋废物。若以印度约30亿辆的车辆保有量推算，优先报废的做法将仅凭可回收材料就产生2.7亿吨废物，此外还会产生540万吨填埋废物，加剧土地和环境资源压力。

在确保安全的前提下，改装通过延长车辆寿命减轻这一负担，从而同时减少材料需求和废物产生。这与联合国可持续发展目标第12项——负责任消费和生产——的契合并非偶然。改装直接支持建立可持续消费模式、提高资源效率和减少废物的要求。

报废通过从确实达到使用寿命终点的车辆中回收材料来推动循环性；改装则通过防止结构完好的车辆过早进入这一阶段来推动循环性。两者缺一不可，问题在于每辆车应走哪条路径。

政策应根据车辆状况而非仅凭车龄来制定。一个有益的起点是建立全国车辆分级框架，区分三种不同路径。第一条路径适用于仍然安全、合规且效率良好的车辆。这类车辆应通过日常维护继续运营。并非每辆老旧车辆都有问题，不能仅凭车龄就将其停用。

第二条路径是改装，适用于结构完好但动力总成老化、效率低下或污染严重的车辆。这类车辆可通过认证的转换流程改造为电动汽车，在延长使用寿命的同时减少排放和对化石燃料的依赖。

第三条路径是报废和回收，仅适用于安全受到影响、结构严重劣化、遭受事故损坏、腐蚀严重，或继续运营存在不安全风险的车辆。

这样的分级框架将使印度的交通转型与真正的循环经济原则相契合。它将承认车辆状况各不相同，政策必须区分已经耗尽价值的资产与仍具有较高使用价值的资产。

印度交通部门的转型并非新电动汽车与老旧车辆之间的竞争，而是一个关于印度如何在能源转型中实现资源效率的问题。

循环经济分级体系的存在有其必然原因：它在废物产生之前加以预防，只有当产品确实达到使用寿命终点后才进行回收。这一区分可以避免不必要的报废。如果印度采用以车龄评估为基础的转型路径，就表明其真正理解了这一循环性原则。

此举还将使报废政策更容易被接受，因为公民会认识到老旧车辆不会受到不加区分的淘汰，而会先接受其改造潜力的评估。它将推动真正循环性的实现。

印度正成为全球能源转型的引领者，也可以在如何管理转型方面发挥领导作用。不仅要依靠减少废物，更要依靠智慧。这不仅仅是可持续性，而是使印度经济历经数百年依然保持韧性的原则。

（Jaideep Saraswat是Vasudha Foundation清洁电力、电动交通与新兴技术业务领域的副总监，Ashish Dokania是Green Tiger Mobility Private Limited首席执行官。作者声明不存在利益冲突。）

Unlock these with Subscription Days after Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu visited Pakistan for a bilateral visit that yielded many agreements, the former Foreign Minister of Maldives, Abdulla Shahid, accused him of moving in an “anti- India ” direction. Also read | Defence pacts with India being amended, says Maldives Mr. Shahid, who is running for the leadership of the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP) ahead of the Presidential elections in 2028, alleged that Mr. Muizzu, who has had a cordial relationship with New Delhi for most of his tenure, would revive the “India Out” campaign of 2023. “The President [Mr. Muizzu] is trying to make India the issue again, because for him, he hasn’t been able to perform. He hasn’t been able to provide any development or deliver on any of the promises, and therefore, come next election again, he will try to create some narrative on hate,” Mr. Shahid, who was Foreign Minister during the tenure of the previous President Ibrahim Solih (2018-2023) and won a term as the President of the UN General Assembly with India’s support in 2021, told The Hindu in an interview here. The Maldives government spokesperson did not reply to a request for a response to Mr. Shahid’s comments. Mr. Shahid called for more transparency about 20 MoUs signed between the Maldives and Pakistan when President Muizzu went on a three-day visit to Islamabad from October 20 to 22, the first such visit by a Maldives President since 2015. After talks between Mr. Muizzu and Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the two sides announced agreements in a number of areas, including defence and maritime security, combating illicit trafficking and narcotics, information technology, cybersecurity and AI. They agreed to start direct flights between Male and Islamabad. In particular, Mr. Muizzu’s meeting with Pakistan’s Field Marshal and Army chief General Asim Munir had raised eyebrows in Delhi. Mr. Muizzu also called for the revival of SAARC, on hold since 2016 when India pulled out of the summit in Islamabad over cross-border terrorism. “We do not want Maldives to be drawn into disputes within our neighbours,” said Mr. Shahid, demanding that the Muizzu government make a statement in Parliament about the nature of the agreements signed with Pakistan. “We must aim for expanding our relationship with everyone who has goodwill to the Maldives, but it should not come at the cost of our own friends, our established relationships,” he added. When asked about Mr. Muizzu’s Pakistan visit on Friday, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that the government kept a “close watch” on such developments and would “take whatever appropriate steps may be necessary”. In response to the comments on SAARC, Mr. Jaiswal said that it was “one country”, indicating Pakistan, that had “stalled” the functioning of SAARC, and India was keen to strengthen regional cooperation. Mr. Shahid’s comments to The Hindu indicate that ties with India may once again become an issue in the Maldivian elections. Mr. Solih lost the elections in 2023 due to the “India Out” campaign of the People’s National Congress (PNC), led by Mr. Muizzu, against what he alleged was undue Indian influence in the island chain, especially accusing the Solih government of allowing India to build military bases in infrastructure projects that India had constructed. Mr. Muizzu had also demanded that Indian Air Force personnel stationed at three locations in the Maldives, including Gan Island and Hanimadhoo Atoll, who operated aircraft that India had provided to the Maldives, be removed. While the beginning of Mr. Muizzu’s tenure saw tensions with the Modi government, and he chose to travel to Turkiye, the UAE, and China before visiting India, relations improved after India agreed to withdraw military personnel and replace them with civilian personnel instead. In June 2024, a month after the final batch of 89 Indian personnel had been withdrawn, Mr. Muizzu visited India to attend Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s swearing-in ceremony, and then returned in October 2024 for a bilateral visit, when India offered the Maldives several economic support measures, including a currency swap agreement to help Maldives avoid a debt failure. Mr. Shahid, who is standing for the primary elections in the MDP next year, is expected to face some tough competition from his other former colleagues in the cabinet as well, including former Economic Minister Fayyaz Ismail, who has the backing of the current MDP chief and former Maldivian President Mohamed Nasheed. Mr. Shahid and Mr. Solih were rivals of Mr. Nasheed during the previous government, but the opposition has come together within the MDP in order to fight against the ruling PNC. The run-up to the 2028 elections has heated up after the PNC confirmed Mr. Muizzu for the 2028 ticket, and the MDP held its party congress, endorsing the “Big Change” ticket for constitutional reform proposed by Mr. Ismail. Mr. Shahid is in India to attend the Words Beyond Borders International Literature Festival and is expected to affirm a campaign more friendly to India. When asked whether he would back an “India-first” campaign like Mr. Solih did, Mr. Shahid said his outreach would always be “first to India” on foreign policy, but not on domestic issues, which were sovereign. “India has always been our first responder. India has always been a generous partner in development. India is our immediate neighbour, who has been consistent in its relationship with the Maldives. So, our history proves the relationship right,” he said, referring to close ties between India and the Maldives since 1965, when the Maldives won its independence from British rule. Hindu》发表的言论表明，与印度的关系可能再次成为马尔代夫选举中的议题。2023年，索利赫在穆伊祖领导的国民大会党（PNC）发起“印度离开”运动后输掉选举。该党指责印度对马尔代夫群岛施加不当影响，尤其指责索利赫政府允许印度在印度出资建设的基础设施项目中修建军事基地。穆伊祖还要求撤走驻扎在马尔代夫三个地点的印度空军人员，包括甘岛和哈尼马杜环礁；这些人员使用印度提供给马尔代夫的飞机。穆伊祖任期初期与莫迪政府关系紧张，他先访问了土耳其、阿联酋和中国，之后才访问印度。但在印度同意撤走军事人员并以文职人员取代后，双边关系有所改善。2024年6月，在最后一批89名印度人员撤离一个月后，穆伊祖访问印度，出席总理纳伦德拉·莫迪的就职宣誓仪式，并于2024年10月再次进行双边访问。印度当时向马尔代夫提供了多项经济支持措施，包括一项货币互换协议，以帮助马尔代夫避免发生债务违约。沙希德先生计划明年参加MDP初选，预计将受到内阁其他前同僚的激烈竞争，其中包括前经济部长法亚兹·伊斯梅尔，后者得到现任MDP党首、马尔代夫前总统穆罕默德·纳希德的支持。上一届政府时期，沙希德先生与索利赫先生都曾是纳希德先生的竞争对手，但反对派已在MDP内部联合起来，共同对抗执政的PNC。PNC确认穆伊祖参加2028年选举后，竞选活动逐渐升温；MDP召开党代会， 支持伊斯梅尔提出的宪法改革方案及“大变革”竞选主张。沙希德先生目前身在印度，参加Words Beyond Borders国际文学节，预计将公开支持一项对印度更友好的竞选活动。当被问及是否会像索利赫先生那样支持“印度优先”运动时，沙希德先生说，在外交政策上，他的对外联络将始终“首先面向印度”，但在国内问题上不会如此，因为国内事务属于主权范畴。他说：“印度始终是我们的第一响应者。印度始终是发展领域慷慨的伙伴。印度是我们的近邻，与马尔代夫保持着一贯的关系。因此，我们的历史证明双方的关系是正确的。”他指的是，自1965年马尔代夫摆脱英国统治获得独立以来，印度与马尔代夫一直保持密切关系。评论必须以英文提交，并且使用完整句子。评论不得含有辱骂性内容或针对个人的攻击。请遵守我们的社区评论准则。我们已迁移至新的评论平台。如果你已经是《The https://www.thehindu.com/business/econom.body: Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters. This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received. Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered. There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury. Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed. There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics. First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky. The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance. The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth. Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile. Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016. Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage. The proposal is being dressed up as a modest, targeted measure affecting only large-value transactions. But modest measures on payment rails have a way of expanding once the legal architecture exists. Section 10A, once amended, does not expire when this particular MDR proposal is shelved. The better outcome is for the government to leave the payments system alone, let UPI’s network effects keep compounding, and find its revenue elsewhere. 政府刚刚在法律上给自己开了口子，可以对一项耗费十年打造的支付习惯征税。2026年《税收及其他法律（修正案）法案》中纳入了对2007年《支付与结算系统法》第10A条的修正，允许政府就特定电子支付方式公布收费规定。拟议费率为：对超过₹2,000的UPI交易收取0.25%至0.5%的商户折扣费率（MDR）。官方说法称，这一门槛按交易笔数计算仅涉及约5%的交易，因此不会波及占据UPI使用量大部分的牛奶和蔬菜商户付款。但它将覆盖约65%的交易金额，这正是其重要之处。

这不是一项无关紧要的技术性调整。它与一项持续十年的政策承诺背道而驰，值得接受比目前更多的审查。回顾一下政策脉络。2016年11月的现金注销措施，其理由之一就是推动经济减少现金依赖。同年早些时候推出的UPI成为这一推动的载体，其零MDR制度是一项有意实施的补贴，旨在让商户和消费者摆脱现金。效果非常显著。如今，UPI每月处理的交易量超过全球大多数卡支付网络的总和。在成功推动这个国家减少现金使用、转向电子支付之后，政府如今又想削弱自己一手促成的这项成果。

通过政策持续偏袒某一种支付方式、而非其他方式的趋势似乎依然存在。印度长期以来甚至对信用卡征税。信用卡利息和费用须缴纳18%的商品和服务税（GST），使信用卡使用成本不必要地偏高。按国际标准，对循环信贷利息征税并不常见；多数司法管辖区将消费信贷利息视为私人财务成本，而非应税服务。印度却像是在对使用信用卡这一行为本身征收奢侈品税。现在，政府投入政治资本推广的支付通道UPI，也即将受到类似对待。这一模式表明，政府需要制定一套更协调一致的支付政策，而不是屈从于对每笔可观察交易征税的诱惑。

除了观感问题，这项具体举措至少还存在两个问题。第一，基础经济理论告诉我们，税负的征收对象与实际承担成本的人并不总是同一主体。此外，UPI或任何支付界面都是一个双边市场，对双边市场征税确实十分棘手。按照政府的说法，MDR名义上将由商户承担，通过银行和印度国家支付公司（National Payments Corporation of India）的生态系统收取。但这成本究竟会被转嫁给商户、再转嫁给消费者，还是由银行和支付服务提供商吸收，取决于市场两端的竞争强度。银行和金融科技公司都在争夺商户关系，无法轻易提高价格，否则就会把交易量流失给提供免费UPI受理服务的竞争者。

更可能的结果是，由构建并维护支付基础设施的中间机构——银行和支付服务提供商（PSP）——吸收成本，从而削弱它们投资于可靠性、欺诈防范以及向服务不足群体拓展的动力。一项无法可靠转嫁出去的税赋不会凭空消失；它最可能日后表现为服务质量下降或创新速度放缓。如果政府把这项税收称为支持UPI下一阶段增长所必需的举措，那么这种结果完全违背常理。

第二，UPI确实在边缘层面为金融包容作出了实际贡献。它将非正式交易纳入可记录、可追溯的数字轨迹——这正是多年来主张正式化和税收合规的人士一直希望实现的结果。业界也已尝试根据电子支付形成的数字轨迹提供信贷。每一卢比通过UPI而非现金流动，金融机构最终就能看到并利用它来建立消费画像。直接对这一支付通道收费，可能削弱使用它的动力，与长期的金融包容目标背道而驰。

政府不需要从每一笔电子流动的卢比中增加收入；它需要让这些卢比继续以电子方式流动，因为自2016年以来，正是这种方式带来了政府一直追求的金融包容和税收合规红利。理想情况下，采用哪种支付方式应由参与市场的主体依据经济因素作出决定。企业规模、消费者偏好以及使用替代支付系统的相对成本等因素，应决定各方的使用选择。政策干预以及本届政府对现金的持续打击，已经使天平倾向UPI。如今对UPI征税——无论名义税率多低、金额多小——都可能改变其使用模式；如果UPI使用量因此减少，政策制定者不应感到意外。

这项提案被包装成一项温和且有针对性的措施，声称只影响大额交易。但一旦法律框架确立，对支付通道的温和措施往往会不断扩张。第10A条一旦完成修正，即使这项具体的MDR提案被搁置，也不会自动失效。更好的结果是，政府不去干预支付系统，让UPI的网络效应继续累积，并在其他方面寻找收入来源。

https://www.premiumtimesng.com/business/.body: Nigeria and France have called for stronger political leadership, increased financing and concrete commitments to accelerate the implementation of the global target to protect 30 per cent of the world’s land and seas by 2030. The two countries made the call during a Target 3 Action Day at the ongoing 17th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia. As co-chairs of the High Ambition Coalition (HAC) for Nature and People, the countries stressed the need to sustain political commitment and translate global biodiversity pledges into measurable conservation outcomes. HAC is the largest multilateral coalition united to protect nature. With 123 member countries, the coalition is leading the historic effort to conserve and protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land and 30 per cent of the ocean by the year 2030 (“30×30”). This ambitious plan is a key target of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Established in 2023, the permanent HAC for N&P Secretariat has made significant progress in supporting its members to implement this global target, aiming to halt and reverse biodiversity loss and put nature on a path to recovery. Charles Nicolai, who spoke on behalf of the coalition, said political leadership must continue beyond adopting the target at CBD COP15 in Montreal, Canada. “Political leadership did not end in Montreal, when Target 3 was adopted at CBD COP15. It must endure until the target has been collectively achieved,” he said. Mr Nicolai warned that weak political commitment could slow implementation, adding that only four years remained to achieve the 2030 target. “Where leadership falters, implementation slows. With only four years remaining until 2030, we cannot afford to lose momentum,” he said, expressing confidence that the 30×30 target remained achievable. The 30×30 target is a central component of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted in 2022. It calls on countries to ensure that by 2030, at least 30 per cent of terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine areas are effectively conserved and managed. Mr Nicolai said France had used its presidency of the Group of Seven (G7) this year to advance the effective management of marine protected areas. He said G7 environment ministers agreed to make the issue a collective priority and established a dedicated platform to exchange knowledge and best practices to improve the management of protected marine areas. In West Africa, he said, Nigeria had played a leading role in advocating for the 30×30 target, using its diplomatic influence to promote a coordinated approach to expanding and strengthening protected areas on land and at sea. He added that the coalition had organised six regional and global consultations, with support from its secretariat, to identify measures needed to strengthen implementation. The consultations, held through platforms including ChangeNOW, the Our Ocean Conference, and meetings of the Convention’s scientific subsidiary body, helped develop a 30×30 Ministerial Declaration. According to Mr Nicolai, the declaration was designed to renew political leadership and encourage coalition members to make more ambitious commitments. The coalition also presented the declaration and a 30×30 Global Assessment at a Nature Leaders event at the United Nations headquarters, attended by heads of state and ministers from several countries. In her remarks, Sikeade Egbuwalo, Nigeria’s focal point person to the Convention on Biological Diversity, said achieving the target would require coordinated action across governments, communities, businesses and civil society. She described the 30×30 ambition as more than a slogan, saying it represented a commitment to nature, people and future generations. Ms Egbuwalo outlined six guiding principles underpinning the ministerial declaration:g collective responsibility, transparency, effective management, community participation, local implementation and adequate financing. She said governments must demonstrate progress through transparent reporting, including submissions to the World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas and national reports to the CBD. She also warned against treating the target as a numerical exercise, stressing that protected areas must be effectively managed, ecologically connected, representative and well governed. “Quality matters just as much as quantity! It is not enough to draw lines on a map and declare victory,” she said. Ms Egbuwalo further emphasised the need to ensure that Indigenous Peoples and local communities had meaningful roles in conservation decisions, noting their longstanding contributions to protecting nature. She called for stronger national implementation and regional cooperation, including progress toward ratifying and implementing the Agreement on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, known as the BBNJ Agreement. Mrs Egbuwalo identified financing as a major requirement for achieving the 2030 target, particularly in developing countries. “Ambition is wonderful, but ambition without resources will not get us very far,” she said, calling for adequate, accessible and timely funding to translate commitments into conservation outcomes. She urged governments, development partners, businesses, civil society organisations and other stakeholders to sustain the momentum generated at COP17 beyond the conference. Mrs Egbuwalo also announced that the coalition would work towards organising its first 30×30 Global Summit in 2027, providing another platform to assess progress and share successful conservation initiatives. She said the initiative would bring together governments, non-governmental organisations, funders, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, businesses,s and other partners. “30×30 is not a competition over who protects the most. It is a collective mission to ensure that nature wins — and when nature wins, humanity wins!”
https://www.premiumtimesng.com/business/.title_zh: CBD COP17：尼日利亚和法国推动加快落实“30×30”生物多样性目标
https://www.premiumtimesng.com/business/.body_zh: 尼日利亚和法国呼吁加强政治领导、扩大融资并作出具体承诺，以加快落实到2030年保护全球30%陆地和海洋的全球目标。两国是在亚美尼亚埃里温举行的《联合国生物多样性公约》第十七次缔约方大会（CBD COP17）期间举行的“目标3行动日”活动中提出这一呼吁的。作为“自然与人民雄心联盟”（HAC）的共同主席国，两国强调需要维持政治承诺，将全球生物多样性承诺转化为可衡量的保护成果。HAC是致力于保护自然的最大多边联盟。该联盟拥有123个成员国，正引领一项历史性努力，计划到2030年保护全球至少30%的陆地和30%的海洋（“30×30”）。这项雄心勃勃的计划是《昆明—蒙特利尔全球生物多样性框架》的关键目标。HAC自然与人民常设秘书处成立于2023年，在支持成员落实这一全球目标方面取得了显著进展，致力于遏制并扭转生物多样性损失，使自然走上恢复之路。代表联盟发言的Charles Nicolai表示，在加拿大蒙特利尔举行的CBD COP15上通过目标3之后，政治领导力必须继续发挥作用。他说：“政治领导力并未在CBD COP15通过目标3的蒙特利尔画上句号。它必须持续到各方共同实现该目标为止。”Nicolai先生警告说，政治承诺薄弱可能拖慢落实进程，并指出距离实现2030年目标只剩4年。他说：“领导力一旦动摇，落实速度就会放慢。距离2030年只剩4年，我们不能失去势头。”他表示相信“30×30”目标仍然可以实现。“30×30”目标是2022年通过的《昆明—蒙特利尔全球生物多样性框架》的核心组成部分。该框架呼吁各国确保到2030年，至少30%的陆地、内陆水域、沿海和海洋区域得到有效保护和管理。Nicolai先生说，法国今年利用七国集团（G7）主席国身份，推动有效管理海洋保护区。他说，七国集团环境部长同意将这一问题列为集体优先事项，并设立专门平台交流知识和最佳做法，以改进海洋保护区管理。他说，在西非，尼日利亚在倡导“30×30”目标方面发挥了领导作用，利用自身外交影响力推动协调一致的方法，以扩大和加强陆地及海上保护区。他补充说，该联盟在秘书处支持下组织了6场区域和全球磋商，以确定加强落实所需的措施。这些磋商通过ChangeNOW、“我们的海洋大会”以及公约科学附属机构会议等平台举行，协助制定了“30×30”部长宣言。Nicolai先生表示，这份宣言旨在重申政治领导力，并鼓励联盟成员作出更具雄心的承诺。该联盟还在联合国总部举行的自然领袖活动上发布了宣言和《“30×30”全球评估》，多国国家元首和部长出席了活动。尼日利亚《生物多样性公约》联络负责人Sikeade Egbuwalo在讲话中说，实现这一目标需要政府、社区、企业和民间社会采取协调行动。她称“30×30”雄心不只是口号，而代表了对自然、人类和子孙后代的承诺。Egbuwalo女士概述了支撑部长宣言的6项指导原则：集体责任、透明度、有效管理、社区参与、切实落实和充足融资。她说，各国政府必须通过透明报告展示进展，包括向世界保护地和保护区数据库提交资料，以及向CBD提交国家报告。她还警告不要把这一目标视为单纯的数字游戏，强调保护区必须得到有效管理、具有生态连通性、具备代表性并实行良好治理。她说：“质量与数量同等重要！仅仅在地图上画几条线，然后宣布胜利是不够的。”Egbuwalo女士进一步强调，必须确保原住民和当地社区在保护决策中发挥实质性作用，并指出他们长期以来为保护自然作出的贡献。她呼吁加强国家层面落实和区域合作，包括推动批准和实施《 国家管辖范围以外区域海洋生物多样性保护和可持续利用协定》，即BBNJ协定。Egbuwalo女士指出，融资是实现2030年目标的一项主要需求，发展中国家尤其如此。她说：“雄心固然可贵，但没有资源的雄心无法让我们走得太远。”她呼吁提供充足、便捷且及时的资金，将承诺转化为保护成果。她敦促各国政府、发展伙伴、企业、民间社会组织和其他利益相关方维持COP17产生的势头，并在会议结束后继续推动行动。Egbuwalo女士还宣布，该联盟将努力于2027年组织首届“30×30”全球峰会，为评估进展和分享成功保护举措提供另一个平台。她说，该倡议将汇聚各国政府、非政府组织、资金提供方、原住民和当地社区、企业及其他合作伙伴。“‘30×30’不是 competition 看谁保护得更多。它是一项集体使命，确保自然获胜——而自然获胜，人类就会获胜！”

Unlock these with Subscription The administrations of Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli and Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR) districts have stepped up preparedness on Sunday by setting up control rooms and readying relief centres, as a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a cyclone, according to the India Meteorological Department. Visakhapatnam Collector M. Abhishikth Kishore, reviewing arrangements at a videoconference with Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) Commissioner Ketan Garg said the impact could be as severe as that of Cyclone Montha . He directed officers to remain at their places of work. A control room has been set up at the Collectorate, with others planned to be opened at the GVMC office and at zonal and mandal levels. Officials were instructed to monitor reservoir levels, alert residents living on hill slopes and keep relief centres ready. Mr. Garg said that people had earlier been evacuated from seven areas. The Collector directed officials to arrange for the shifting of those residents again. Tree-cutting machines are to be stationed in advance, while the GVMC and APEPDCL were asked to ensure uninterrupted power supply. Ambulances, medical teams and medicines are to be kept ready. Pregnant women nearing delivery are to be moved to hospitals. Fishermen have been advised not to venture into the sea and, tourists and residents were warned against visiting beaches. Special officers have been appointed for each constituency and mandal. The round-the-clock Collectorate control room can be reached on 0891-2590100 and 0891-2590102, said Special Deputy Collector and District Project Manager T. Govindu. In Anakapalli, Collector Vijaya Krishnan said that people of low-lying and coastal areas were to be identified and relocated by the evening of October 26. Relief centres would provide drinking water and food, while medicines would be available for patients with chronic ailments. High-risk pregnant women are to be shifted to health centres. A round-the-clock control room will function at the Collectorate from October 26. Tahsildars and Mandal Parishad Development Officers have been directed to remain stationed at headquarters, with no leave granted. In Alluri Sitharama Raju district, Collector T. Nishanthi said a control room was being set up at the Collectorate in Paderu to ensure public safety and prompt action in emergencies, with similar facilities planned in all mandals. The control rooms will function round-the-clock to monitor the situation and respond to problems faced by the public. Residents were advised to remain alert and take necessary precautions, and to call 08935-293448 to report cyclone-related problems or seek assistance. https://www.myjoyonline.com/imf-delegati.body: A delegation from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has visited the Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) to familiarise itself with the refinery’s operations, assess ongoing rehabilitation works and gain insight into management’s efforts to restore the facility to sustained operational and financial stability. The visit formed part of the IMF team’s engagements with relevant government authorities and selected state-owned enterprises in Ghana to gain a better understanding of their operations, financial positions, challenges and contributions to the national economy. The delegation was led by the IMF’s Ghana Resident Representative, Dr. Adrian Alter, while the TOR team was led by its Managing Director, Mr. Edmond Kombat, Esq. During a meeting with the delegation, Mr. Kombat outlined the operational and financial challenges inherited by the current management, as well as measures introduced since May 2025 to restore confidence in the refinery’s operations and revive its major processing plants. Addressing the delegation, Mr. Kombat emphasised that management had relied on internally generated funds to sustain the refinery’s operations since assuming office. “Since this new management took over, we have not received a dime from government. Every single thing is done through our internally generated funds,” Mr. Kombat said. He explained that management had prioritised financial discipline, operational improvements and the rehabilitation of critical facilities as part of efforts to reposition the refinery for long-term sustainability. Mr. Kombat disclosed that TOR was engaging the government over its outstanding debt obligations, with discussions focusing on possible restructuring and the reconciliation of historical financial commitments between the refinery and the state. According to him, TOR inherited a debt burden of approximately US$517 million, of which about US$120 million is owed to the government. “Out of the US$517 million debt we inherited, we owe about US$120 million to the government. We are trying to restructure our debt with the government,” he explained. The refinery is also engaging other state institutions to resolve outstanding financial obligations between TOR and the respective entities. Management is exploring possible netting-off arrangements to reconcile the obligations and establish the actual financial position of the parties involved. On the refinery’s financial performance, Mr. Kombat disclosed that TOR recorded a profit in the previous year, expressing optimism that the company could sustain profitability in the current and subsequent years. He attributed this positive outlook, in part, to improved macroeconomic stability and ongoing efforts to strengthen the refinery’s operational and financial position. As part of its long-term strategy, management is considering a potential listing of TOR on the Ghana Stock Exchange to attract investment and provide additional capital for the refinery’s operations and expansion. Mr. Kombat explained that a stock market listing could create opportunities for Ghanaian institutions and other investors to acquire shares in the company, providing an additional avenue for raising funds to support its recovery and growth. The IMF delegation also sought clarification on the volume of crude oil processed by TOR, particularly supplies sourced from Ghana’s domestic oil fields. In response, Mr. Kombat indicated that the refinery had processed approximately five million barrels of crude oil, including about two million barrels sourced from Ghanaian fields, with the remainder coming from external sources. He explained that TOR’s first domestic crude supply came from the Jubilee field through a transaction with Vitol, which was fully paid for. He also acknowledged the contribution of the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC), which supplied its share of Ghana’s crude allocation to the refinery. “Our first domestic crude came from the Jubilee field through Vitol, and it was fully paid for. GNPC also gave us its portion of Ghana’s allocation,” Mr. Kombat stated. He further noted that Ghana produces approximately 38 million barrels of crude oil annually, with about 11 million barrels representing the government’s share. The Managing Director expressed hope that GNPC would make its full crude allocation available to TOR for refining by the following year. He said this would improve feedstock availability and support more consistent refinery operations. The delegation also sought to understand the impact of TOR’s resumption of operations on the Ghanaian economy and consumers. In response, Mr. Kombat highlighted the refinery’s contribution to domestic petroleum product availability, price stability, and the country’s ability to withstand disruptions in international petroleum markets. He explained that domestic refining could help reduce Ghana’s exposure to external supply shocks, particularly during periods of geopolitical tension and uncertainty in global oil markets, including the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. He also acknowledged government interventions aimed at cushioning consumers against the effects of changes in petroleum prices, noting the importance of maintaining a reliable domestic supply of petroleum products. Highlighting the refinery’s commercial potential, Mr. Kombat drew attention to TOR’s tank farm, storage infrastructure and product distribution network. He indicated that TOR has approximately one million metric tonnes of storage capacity, which is three times the capacity of the Bulk Oil Storage and Transportation Company (BOST). The Managing Director further explained that TOR is connected to eight privately operated depots, enabling the refinery to pump petroleum products directly to those facilities. He said these arrangements provide additional revenue opportunities for the refinery, alongside other commercial activities, including laboratory services for petroleum product testing. The discussions also covered corporate governance and financial accountability, particularly efforts to clear a six-year backlog of unaudited accounts. Mr. Kombat explained that the Ghana Audit Service had undertaken the audit exercise to address the six-year backlog of outstanding accounts. He added that management intended to appoint an external audit firm at the refinery’s next Annual General Meeting (AGM) to undertake subsequent audits. KPMG had previously conducted audit assignments for the company. The Managing Director also briefed the delegation on improvements in financial reporting and internal controls, staff-related reforms, and measures to sustain crude supply for continued operations. He noted that these initiatives formed part of a broader management strategy to improve accountability, strengthen financial discipline and enhance operational efficiency. The IMF team was further briefed on ongoing efforts to increase the refinery’s processing capacity, rehabilitate other critical units and restore facilities required to support more reliable operations. These interventions are intended to strengthen TOR’s contribution to Ghana’s energy security, improve its financial sustainability and position it to play a more significant role in the country’s petroleum value chain. Following the discussions, the delegation toured parts of the refinery to observe rehabilitated facilities and ongoing engineering works. The tour provided the IMF team with an opportunity to gain first-hand insight into TOR’s operational environment, the progress made under the current management and the work that remains to be completed. Members of the delegation expressed appreciation for the engagement and the opportunity to gain a better understanding of the refinery’s operations and recovery efforts. The visit also provided a platform for TOR management to outline the measures being pursued to restore critical infrastructure, improve financial performance and strengthen the refinery’s contribution to Ghana’s energy security. The Tema Oil Refinery remains Ghana’s premier refinery, serving customers within the country and beyond its borders

国际货币基金组织（IMF）代表团访问了特马石油炼厂（TOR），了解该炼厂的运营情况，评估正在进行的修复工程，并掌握管理层为使这座设施恢复持续运营和财务稳定所作的努力。此次访问是IMF团队与加纳相关政府主管部门和部分国有机构展开交流的一部分，旨在更好地了解这些机构的运营情况、财务状况、面临的挑战及其对国家经济的贡献。代表团由IMF驻加纳常驻代表阿德里安·阿尔特博士带队，TOR代表团则由总经理埃德蒙·孔巴特先生带队。孔巴特先生在会见代表团期间介绍了现任管理层所继承的运营和财务挑战，以及自2025年5月以来为恢复外界对炼厂运营的信心、重新启动其主要加工装置而推出的各项措施。孔巴特先生向代表团强调，管理层自上任以来一直依靠内部产生的资金维持炼厂运营。孔巴特先生说：“新管理层接手以来，我们没有从政府获得一分钱。每一件事都是用我们内部产生的资金完成的。”他解释道，作为为炼厂重新定位、实现长期可持续发展的努力的一部分，管理层已将财务纪律、运营改善和关键设施修复列为优先事项。孔巴特先生透露，TOR正就其未偿债务义务与政府进行磋商，讨论重点包括可能进行债务重组，以及理清炼厂与国家之间历史遗留的财务承诺。他表示，TOR继承了约US$517 million的债务负担，其中约US$120 million欠付政府。孔巴特先生解释道：“我们继承的US$517 million债务中，约有US$120 million欠付政府。我们正试图与政府重组债务。”该炼厂还在与其他国家机构交涉，以解决TOR与相关实体之间未结清的财务义务。管理层正在研究可能的债务抵扣安排，以理清各项义务并确定相关各方的实际财务状况。在炼厂财务表现方面，孔巴特先生透露，TOR上一年度实现盈利，并乐观预计公司能够在本年度及此后数年保持盈利。他表示，这一积极前景部分得益于宏观经济稳定性有所改善，以及持续加强炼厂运营和财务地位的努力。作为长期战略的一部分，管理层正考虑让TOR在加纳证券交易所上市，以吸引投资并为炼厂运营和扩建提供更多资本。孔巴特先生解释道，股票上市可让加纳境内机构和其他投资者有机会认购公司股份，为支持炼厂复苏和增长提供另一条筹资渠道。IMF代表团还要求说明TOR原油加工量，尤其是来自加纳本土油田的供应量。对此，孔巴特先生表示，该炼厂已加工约500万桶原油，其中约200万桶来自加纳油田，其余来自外部来源。他解释道，TOR首批国产原油通过与Vitol的交易从朱比利油田获得，相关款项已经全部付清。他还肯定了加纳国家石油公司（GNPC）的贡献，该公司向炼厂供应了加纳原油配额中应归其所有的部分。孔巴特先生说：“我们的首批国产原油来自朱比利油田，由Vitol提供，相关款项已经全部付清。GNPC也向我们提供了加纳原油配额中应归其所有的部分。”他进一步指出，加纳每年生产约3800万桶原油，其中约1100万桶代表政府份额。总经理希望，到次年GNPC能够将其全部原油配额供应给TOR进行加工。他表示，这将改善原料供应情况，并支持炼厂更加稳定地运营。代表团还希望了解TOR恢复运营对加纳经济和消费者的影响。对此，孔巴特先生强调，该炼厂有助于保障国内石油产品供应、维护价格稳定，并增强加纳抵御国际石油市场供应中断的能力。他解释道，国内炼油能够降低加纳受外部供应冲击影响的程度，尤其是在地缘政治紧张以及全球石油市场存在不确定性的时期，包括中东持续冲突期间。他还提到，政府采取了干预措施，以缓冲消费者受到石油价格变化影响的冲击，同时强调维持国内石油产品可靠供应的重要性。在谈及炼厂的商业潜力时，孔巴特先生提请注意TOR的储油罐区、储存基础设施和产品配送网络。他表示，TOR拥有约100万吨的储存能力，是散装油储存与运输公司（BOST）储存能力的3倍。总经理进一步解释道，TOR与8座私营油库相连，使炼厂能够将石油产品直接输送至这些设施。他说，除了其他商业活动，包括为石油产品检测提供实验室服务，这些安排也为炼厂带来了额外的收入机会。会议还讨论了公司治理和财务问责问题，尤其是清理长达6年的未经审计账目积压。孔巴特先生解释道，加纳审计署已开展审计工作，以处理积压6年的未结账目。他补充说，管理层计划在炼厂下一次年度股东大会（AGM）上聘任一家外部审计事务所，负责后续审计。KPMG此前曾为公司执行审计任务。总经理还向代表团介绍了财务报告和内部控制、员工相关改革，以及维持原油供应以保障持续运营等方面取得的进展。他指出，这些举措是更广泛管理战略的一部分，战略目标是加强问责、强化财务纪律和提升运营效率。IMF团队还听取了有关持续努力情况的介绍，这些努力包括提高炼厂加工能力、修复其他关键装置，以及恢复支持更可靠运营所需的设施。这些干预措施旨在加强TOR对加纳能源安全的贡献，提高其财务可持续性，并使其能够在加纳石油价值链中发挥更重要的作用。讨论结束后，代表团参观了炼厂的部分区域，观察已修复的设施和正在进行的工程作业。此次参观使IMF团队得以实地了解TOR的运营环境、现任管理层取得的进展以及尚待完成的工作。代表团成员对此次交流以及深入了解炼厂运营和复苏努力的机会表示赞赏。此次访问也为TOR管理层提供了一个平台，用于介绍其为恢复关键基础设施、改善财务表现以及加强炼厂对加纳能源安全贡献而采取的措施。特马石油炼厂仍是加纳最主要的炼厂，为加纳境内及境外客户提供服务……

https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.title: What can be done to curb ‘paper leaks’ and ensure institutional accountability?
https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.summary: In such an environment, paper leaks and other irregularities have repeatedly surfaced, though they are often collectively described simply as “paper leaks.” The controversies surrounding NEET-2024, UGC-NET 2024, and NEET-2026 triggered unprecedented national concern.
https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.summary_zh: 在这样的环境中，试卷泄题及其他不当行为屡次曝光，尽管人们通常统称其为“试卷泄题”。围绕NEET-2024、UGC-NET 2024和NEET-2026的争议引发了前所未有的全国关注。
https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.body: Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription NEET is one of India’s highest-stakes examinations, where intense competition, immense social prestige, and the multi-crore value of a medical seat generate enormous academic, financial, and psychological pressure. Similar pressures surround other national admission, scholarship and recruitment examinations. In such an environment, paper leaks and other irregularities have repeatedly surfaced, though they are often collectively described simply as “paper leaks.” The controversies surrounding NEET-2024, UGC-NET 2024, and NEET-2026 triggered unprecedented national concern. UGC-NET 2024 was canceled and held again, while NEET 2026 was also re-conducted. All three were conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA), which attributed these decisions to specific external or intelligence inputs. The CBI investigated the NEET-2024 and UGC-NET 2024 cases. Although the investigations initially led to arrests and extensive nationwide media coverage, the CBI has since submitted closure reports in both cases, reportedly finding no prosecutable evidence of a conventional paper leak under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, or the Public Examinations Act (PEA), 2024. The NEET-2026 investigation remains in progress, with a chargesheet already filed. These developments raise a more fundamental question: if repeated examination crises ultimately yield no prosecutable evidence of a conventional paper leak, what exactly constitutes a “paper leak”? Where do such compromises originate, and who is responsible for detecting, preventing, and being held accountable for them? Traditionally, a “paper leak” refers to the unauthorised disclosure of a printed question paper before the examination, typically during printing, packaging, storage, or transportation. Investigation protocols, therefore, focus on tracing printed papers and recovering physical evidence. The recent Maharashtra Teachers Eligibility Test (TET) case is a classic example in which coded printed question papers were allegedly leaked from a compromised printing press. High-stakes examinations, however, present a far more complex picture. Long before printing, questions pass through question-setting, moderation, translation, digitisation, and final compilation, where a limited number of individuals have privileged access. Compromises at any of these stages may never result in a leaked printed paper. Yet, it can selectively disclose questions or other confidential material, providing an unfair advantage to a few candidates before spreading through organised networks. The NEET and UGC-NET controversies illustrate this distinction. Although investigations reportedly found no evidence of leaked printed papers in the 2024 cases, the examinations nevertheless led to arrests, cancellations, re-examinations, and a crisis of public confidence. Similarly, the circulation of highly targeted “guided papers” before NEET-2026 raised questions about whether confidential information had flowed through insider or informal networks despite the absence of any recovered printed paper. Examination compromise may therefore involve far more than a printed paper: selected questions, question banks, recurring themes, high-probability question pools, examiner identities, confidential instructions, digital data, or administrative information may all be unlawfully disclosed through insider access, cyber intrusions, or coaching networks. Restricting the definition of a “paper leak” to a leaked printed question paper overlooks these significant vulnerabilities. In this context, extraordinary measures such as transporting the re-NEET 2026 question papers by aircraft may secure the final logistical stage but do little to address vulnerabilities at the source. The real issue is whether confidential examination information was disclosed in any form that compromised the fairness, integrity, or credibility of the examination. A leaked printed question paper is only one form of examination compromise. The integrity of an examination may be undermined equally by failures before, during, or after the examination, even when no printed paper is ever recovered. NEET-2024 illustrates this broader spectrum. Reported irregularities included the distribution of an incorrect question paper, followed by its replacement; delayed collection or replacement of OMR sheets; exceptional grace marks; tie-breaking disputes; clustering of near-perfect scores; and unusually high scores from certain centres and coaching hubs. Collectively, these exposed weaknesses in examination management and institutional oversight. Other breaches include cybersecurity failures, manipulation of candidate or examination data, disclosure of confidential information, compromised examination centres, impersonation, organised unfair means, and insider access or coaching-network access to privileged information. Safeguarding public examinations, therefore, requires securing the entire examination lifecycle — from question development to result processing — rather than focusing solely on recovering leaked printed papers. Failures in the transport of printed question papers alone cannot explain many examination breaches. Critical processes—including question selection, paper allocation, examination-centre management, OMR handling, grace marks, result processing, cybersecurity, and access to confidential data—are controlled by the examination authority and its associated agencies. Irregularities at these stages naturally raise questions about institutional controls and insider vulnerabilities. The NEET-2024 controversy illustrates this broader picture. Distribution of an incorrect question paper, delayed OMR handling, exceptional grace marks, unusually high scores from certain centres, and the circulation of highly targeted “guided papers” all point to vulnerabilities that extend beyond conventional paper leaks. Such patterns warrant scrutiny of repeated expert engagement, conflicts of interest, links to coaching ecosystems, and other insider risks. This does not imply that every irregularity results from insider misconduct. However, securing examinations requires protecting confidential information, institutional processes, and printed question papers alike. Preventing examination breaches cannot be left to the CBI, police, or courts, which act only after a crisis. Primary responsibility lies with the examination authority, supported by the Ministry of Education, intelligence, and cybersecurity agencies, and independent oversight. Accountability should extend across the entire examination lifecycle — from the selection of question setters and translators to examination centres, digital systems, evaluation, and result processing. It requires rigorous antecedent verification, conflict-of-interest scrutiny, periodic rotation of experts, cybersecurity audits, intelligence-based monitoring, and clear audit trails. Ultimately, the credibility of a public examination depends not on post-facto arrests or the recovery of a leaked printed paper, but on the ability of institutions to prevent breaches before they occur and sustain public confidence in the integrity of the entire process. The official response to the NEET-2024, UGC-NET 2024, and NEET-2026 controversies has largely rested on the absence of conclusive evidence of a conventional paper leak. Before the Supreme Court, the NTA attributed the cancellation and re-conduct of NEET-2026 to specific intelligence inputs, while the High-Powered Steering Committee emphasised compliance with its recommendations and SOPs. The CBI’s investigations into NEET-2024 and UGC-NET 2024 resulted in closure reports, reportedly finding no prosecutable evidence of a paper leak and no basis to prosecute NTA officials. The NEET-2026 investigation, however, remains ongoing. These official positions contrast sharply with the ground reality. Cancelled or re-conducted examinations, arrests, allegations of widely circulated “guided papers”, cyber-security incidents, operational lapses, and disruptions affecting millions of candidates. In NEET-2026, official action reportedly followed a whistleblower’s FIR rather than detection through the examination’s own security or intelligence systems. This raises an obvious question: if no credible abnormality was detected, what justified cancelling NEET-2026? Conversely, if credible intelligence existed, why did institutional safeguards fail to detect or prevent the compromise beforehand? Until these questions are answered transparently, stronger logistics or harsher penal laws alone are unlikely to restore public confidence. The priority must shift from post-crisis response to institutional prevention. As its first task, the newly constituted committee headed by former UIDAI chairman Nandan Nilekani should prepare a comprehensive White Paper documenting the full spectrum of breaches in NEET-2024, UGC-NET 2024, and NEET-2026—covering leakages, operational failures, cybersecurity incidents, centre-level irregularities, investigations, judicial outcomes, and lessons learned. Honest diagnosis must precede meaningful reform. The White Paper should underpin a Public Examination Integrity Framework (PEIF) for all major examination bodies. The Framework should prescribe standardised end-to-end SOPs covering the entire examination lifecycle, with an emphasis on conflict-of-interest management, expert selection, cybersecurity, examination administration, audit, and institutional accountability. Ultimately, public confidence will be restored not by tougher laws or more post-facto investigations, but by an examination system that detects risks early, prevents breaches before they occur, and ensures institutional accountability. https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.title_zh: 如何遏制“泄题”，并确保制度问责？
https://www.thehindu.com/education/what-.body_zh: 订阅可享受更多权益，包括《Premium Stories》《Editorials》《Opinions》等内容。解锁这些内容需订阅。NEET是印度竞争最激烈的考试之一，竞争激烈、社会声望极高，一张医学席位价值数千万卢比，由此带来巨大的学业、经济和心理压力。其他全国性入学、奖学金和招聘考试也面临类似压力。在这样的环境中，泄题及其他违规行为屡次浮现，但人们往往统称为“泄题”。围绕NEET-2024、UGC-NET 2024和NEET-2026的争议引发了前所未有的全国关注。UGC-NET 2024被取消后重新举行，NEET 2026也重新组织。三场考试均由国家测试局（NTA）举办，该机构称这些决定源于具体的外部情报或情报信息。中央调查局（CBI）调查了NEET-2024和UGC-NET 2024两案。尽管调查最初导致逮捕，并在全国媒体上进行了广泛报道，但CBI此后已就两案提交结案报告，据称未发现依据2023年《印度刑法》或2024年《公共考试法》可以提起公诉的传统泄题证据。NEET-2026的调查仍在进行，控告书已经提交。这些进展提出了一个更根本的问题：如果反复发生的考试危机最终都没有产生可依法起诉的传统泄题证据，那么究竟什么才算“泄题”？此类妥协行为源自何处？谁负责发现、预防并追究其责任？传统意义上的“泄题”，是指在考试前未经授权泄露纸质试题，通常发生在印刷、包装、储存或运输环节。因此，调查程序往往侧重于追踪纸质试卷并寻找实物证据。最近的Maharashtra教师资格测试（TET）案就是一个典型例子，据称加密编码的纸质试题从遭渗透的印刷机构泄露。然而，高风险考试所呈现的情况要复杂得多。在印刷之前，试题要经过命题、审核、翻译、数字化和最终汇编等环节，在此期间，少数人员拥有特权访问权限。这些环节中的任何妥协行为都可能不会产生纸质试卷泄露，却可能选择性泄露试题或其他机密材料，在通过有组织的网络扩散之前，先让少数考生获得不公平优势。NEET和UGC-NET争议恰好说明了这之间的区别。尽管据称调查未在2024年两案中发现纸质试卷泄露的证据，但考试仍导致逮捕、取消、重考以及公众信任危机。同样，NEET-2026前流通的高度定向“押题卷”引发了疑问：在没有找回任何纸质试卷的情况下，机密信息是否通过内部人员或非正式网络流出？因此，考试妥协可能远不止于纸质试卷。特定试题、题库、反复出现的出题模式、高概率题池、命题人身份、机密指示、数字数据或行政信息，都可能通过内部访问、网络入侵或辅导网络被非法泄露。如果把“泄题”的定义局限于纸质试题泄露，就会忽视这些重大风险漏洞。在这一背景下，采取非常措施，例如用飞机运送重新举行的NEET 2026试题，或许能够守住最后的物流环节，却几乎无法消除源头漏洞。真正的问题在于，机密考试信息是否以任何形式被披露，从而破坏考试的公平、公正或公信力。纸质试卷泄露只是考试妥协的一种形式。即使始终未能找回纸质试卷，考试前、考试中或考试后的失误同样会削弱考试的完整性。NEET-2024体现了这一更广泛的失范现象。据报道，相关违规行为包括发放错误试卷后予以更换、延迟收取或更换答题卡、给予异常宽限分、同分判定争议、近满分成绩扎堆，以及某些考点和辅导机构出现异常高分。这些现象共同暴露了考试管理和机构监督方面的薄弱环节。其他违规行为还包括网络安全失效、考生或考试数据被操纵、机密信息披露、考试中心被攻破、冒名顶替、有组织的不公平舞弊，以及内部人员或辅导网络获得特权信息。因此，维护公共考试的安全，需要保护从试题开发到成绩处理的整个考试生命周期，而不是只专注于追回泄露的纸质试卷。仅凭纸质试卷运输环节的失误，无法解释许多考试违规行为。试题遴选、试卷分配、考试中心管理、答题卡处理、宽限分、成绩处理、网络安全以及机密数据访问等关键流程，均由考试主管机构及其相关机构掌控。这些环节出现违规，自然会引发对机构内部控制和内部人员风险的疑问。NEET-2024争议更能说明这一全貌。错误试卷的发放、答题卡处理延迟、异常宽限分、某些考点出现异常高分，以及高度定向“押题卷”的流通，都表明漏洞超出了传统泄题的范围。此类模式有必要审查专家反复参与的情况、利益冲突、与辅导生态的关联以及其他内部风险。这并不意味着每项异常都源于内部人员的不当行为。然而，要保障考试安全，就必须同时保护机密信息、机构流程和纸质试卷。防止考试违规不能只交给CBI、警察或法院，因为这些机构都是在危机发生后才介入。主要责任在于考试主管机构，并在教育部、情报机构和网络安全机构以及独立监督机制的支持下履行。问责应覆盖整个考试生命周期，从遴选命题人和翻译人员延伸至考试中心、数字系统、阅卷和成绩处理。相关制度需要严格的事前核查、利益冲突审查、专家定期轮换、网络安全审计、基于情报的监测，以及清晰的审计轨迹。归根结底，公共考试的可信度并不取决于事后逮捕或追回泄露的纸质试卷，而取决于各机构能否在违规发生前予以预防，并持续维护公众对整个考试流程完整性的信心。针对NEET-2024、UGC-NET 2024和NEET-2026争议，官方应对主要依据是缺乏传统泄题的确凿证据。在最高法院上，NTA称取消并重新举行NEET-2026源于具体情报信息，而高级别指导委员会则强调须遵守其建议和标准操作程序。CBI对NEET-2024和UGC-NET 2024的调查形成了结案报告，据称未发现泄题的可起诉证据，也没有起诉NTA官员的依据。然而，NEET-2026的调查仍在继续。这些官方立场与社会现实形成鲜明反差：考试被取消或重新举行、人员遭到逮捕、有人指称“押题卷”大范围流传、发生网络安全事件、运营失误，以及影响数百万考生的中断。在NEET-2026中，据称官方行动源于举报人的第一份举报，而不是通过考试自身的安全或情报系统发现异常。这就引出了一个显而易见的问题：如果没有发现可信的异常情况，取消NEET-2026的依据是什么？反之，如果确有可信情报，为何机构的安全保障未能事先发现或阻止妥协行为？在这些问题得到透明回答之前，仅靠加强物流或加重刑罚，不太可能恢复公众信心。工作重点必须从危机后应对转向机构预防。新组建的委员会由前UIDAI主席Nandan Nilekani牵头，其首要任务应是编制一份全面白皮书，记录NEET-2024、UGC-NET 2024和NEET-2026中各种违规失范现象，涵盖泄题、运营失误、网络安全事件、考点层面的异常、调查结果、司法裁判结果及经验教训。诚实诊断必须先于实质性改革。白皮书应成为面向所有主要考试机构的《公共考试诚信框架》（PEIF）的基础。该框架应规定覆盖整个考试生命周期的标准化端到端标准操作程序，重点涵盖利益冲突管理、专家遴选、网络安全、考试管理、审计和机构问责。归根结底，恢复公众信心的办法不是更严厉的法律或更多事后调查，而是一套能够尽早发现风险、在违规发生前加以预防，并确保机构问责的考试体系。评论必须使用英文，并以完整句子表述。评论不得包含辱骂性或人身攻击内容。请遵守我们的社区评论准则。我们已迁移至新的评论平台。如果你已是The Unlock these with Subscription District Collector Dineshan Cheruvatt has extended the ban on vehicular traffic on the Adimaly–Munnar stretch of the Kochi–Dhanushkodi National Highway for another two weeks on Saturday following another major landslip at Karadippara, near Moonammile, in the Munnar hill station. Officials said traffic was suspended on the route last Monday after a landslip occurred during highway-widening work. National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) officials subsequently began clearing rock and debris, expecting to complete the work within a week. However, during the clearing operations, a huge quantity of rock and debris fell onto the highway on Friday evening, damaging the retaining wall on the lower stretch of the road. Following the incident, the district administration decided to extend the complete traffic ban for another two weeks. A senior Revenue department official said loose rock and soil were continuing to slide down during the clearing operations. “When rockfalls occur, large masses of rock and trees are left perched at the top without any grip. The debris continues to fall onto the road during the work. Without fully removing the debris, we cannot resume traffic on the highway. In addition, the retaining wall must be rebuilt. The NHAI has been directed to speed up the work. We expect to complete the work within two weeks,” the official said. Meanwhile, sources noted that clearing the debris and rebuilding the protection wall after the second landslip remains a major challenge that could take longer than anticipated. Last week, following the initial landslip, traffic on the highway was diverted along alternative routes. Motorists travelling from Adimaly to Munnar was asked to divert at Iruttukanam and proceed via Anachal and Randammile to reach Munnar. Those heading from Munnar to Adimaly were asked to take the reverse Randammile–Anachal–Iruttukanam route. Travellers headed toward Mankulam were asked to divert at Iruttukanam to reach Kallar Junction before turning onto the Mankulam road. According to officials, motorists must continue using these alternative routes while the full ban remains in place. “Without imposing a complete traffic ban, the authorities cannot safely continue the debris removal and road-strengthening work,” the official added. Unlock these with Subscription The West Bengal Cabinet has approved the permanent transfer of 31.905 acres at nine locations to the Border Security Force (BSF) for border fencing and related security infrastructure, along with 1.53 acres for three new Border Outposts in Malda, Nadia and Cooch Behar. Reported in early June 2026, the decision was presented as part of the State government’s efforts to strengthen surveillance and infrastructure along the India-Bangladesh border. The decision does not represent a new border policy but the release of land that had remained pending despite repeated administrative and judicial intervention. It removes a major State-level bottleneck in a long-delayed border infrastructure project affected by land acquisition disputes, difficult terrain, and legal and political complications. The move also follows the Calcutta High Court’s order of January 2026, delivered by Chief Justice Sujoy Paul and Justice Partha Sarathi Sen in WPA (P) 45 of 2025, Lt. Gen. (Retd.) Dr. Subrata Saha v. Union of India & Others, directing the State government to hand over acquired land in nine border districts to the BSF by March 31, 2026, observing that land already acquired or compensated should not remain unused for border fencing.
